text: Chapter 1 has gone image-first so far — layers, Dockerfiles, multi-stage builds. A real application is rarely one container, though, it's usually an API container talking to a database container, maybe a cache container too. This lesson covers what makes that actually work: containers finding each other over the network, and data surviving a container restart.

Every container lands on a network at startup, and if you don't specify one, that's Docker's default bridge — where containers can reach each other by IP, but not by name. Create your own network instead with docker network create, and Docker runs embedded DNS for it automatically. Attach a Postgres container and an API container to that same network by name, and the API container's connection string can reference the hostname db directly — no hardcoded IP, no breaking when a container restarts with a new one.

A container's writable layer disappears the moment you remove it, so a database's actual files can't live there. A named volume is storage Docker itself manages under a name, mounted into the container with -v, and it survives docker rm until you deliberately run docker volume rm. A bind mount instead maps a specific host path straight into the container, making the host filesystem the live source of truth — exactly what you want for editing source code during local development.

Running containers by hand with matching network and volume flags works, but docker-compose.yml expresses the same multi-container app declaratively. docker compose up creates a project network automatically, so db and api can already resolve each other by service name with no extra configuration. depends_on controls start order only, not readiness, so an application still needs its own retry logic for a database that's started but not yet accepting connections.

That closes out Chapter 1: real layers underneath every image, a Dockerfile that builds fast and stays small, a multi-stage build that keeps the toolchain out of what ships, and now networking and volumes that let several containers work together as one real local application. Chapter 2 moves beyond a single Docker host, into what changes once Kubernetes is scheduling and networking containers across an entire cluster.
